name: Elena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brannock and Sons, a family builder in our town, and I've been with them twenty-two years. We do house extensions, garages, garden rooms, the odd barn conversion. This month it's a two-storey extension behind a farmhouse on Church Lane, and I'm doing the floor joists, the stud walls and the stairs. I like a job you can stand back from at the end of the day and see what you've done, and I don't like the cold getting into my hands in the mornings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about who you work with and your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Old Mr Brannock taught me the trade, and now his son Rob runs it. There's six of us, and we've all known each other for years, I was at Rob's wedding. Outside work it's church on Sunday, I sing in the choir at St Michael's, and Saturdays I have two of the grandchildren. I don't touch the AI things, I've got a phone because Henrik insisted, and that's for ringing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Well, I could have told them that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you are, all that fuss for nothing. Good honest work is still good honest work. I'd say that after church as much as anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish out my years with Brannock the way I always meant to. Eight more years, God willing, then hand over to the youngsters. That's all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep on as I am. Work at Brannock, sing on Sundays, look after the little ones on Saturday. Keep putting away what we can, we've got about three months put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hand over to the youngsters. Who are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob's taken on an apprentice, Owen, he's seventeen and keen as anything. I'm teaching him to cut a stair string, the way Mr Brannock taught me. That's how a trade should pass on, hand to hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there'll be enough work for a small firm like ours. The big builders get the council land and we get the extensions. But we've always got by, people round here like to use someone they know.

S0.say: There you are, all that fuss for nothing. Good honest work is still good honest work, and I'd say that after church as much as anywhere.
S0.think: I can finish my years with Brannock the way I always meant to. Eight more years, God willing, then hand over to the youngsters.
S0.do: Carries on working at Brannock, singing on Sundays and minding grandchildren on Saturdays. Keeps adding to about three months of savings.
S0.quote: I'm teaching him to cut a stair string, the way Mr Brannock taught me. That's how a trade should pass on, hand to hand.
S0.fieldNote: Her identity rests on passing the trade on through apprenticeship. She is deeply rooted in a small family firm and her church. A plateau confirms what she already believed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, many jobs. Hmm. That's the big firms you're talking about, I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful what they wish for. Every new thing has a cost, and it's usually ordinary people who pay it. But I'd also say a small firm like Brannock will carry on, because people want a builder they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it would pass Brannock by for a while, Rob's not going to spend money on gadgets he doesn't need. My worry is Owen. If the big firms need fewer apprentices, where do young lads like him learn a trade?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I'd keep working and keep my head down. If Rob said we had to use some new tablet, I'd ask Owen to show me and grumble about it. I'd wait and see what it really does before I worried more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me, for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if apprentices got squeezed out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that sell this stuff, and the people in cities who decide things without ever setting foot on a building site. They talk about progress, but they're not the ones who'll have a seventeen-year-old with nowhere to go. And the government, if it pays people to sit at home instead of paying firms to train them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Owen to show you. Isn't that the opposite of how it usually goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd laugh about it. I teach him the stairs and he teaches me the screen. Fair's fair, I suppose, though I'd still rather do it my way.

S1.say: People should be careful what they wish for, because ordinary people usually pay for new things. But a small firm like Brannock will carry on, because people want a builder they know.
S1.think: I think it would pass Brannock by for a while, since Rob won't spend on gadgets he doesn't need. My worry is Owen: if the big firms need fewer apprentices, where do lads like him learn a trade?
S1.do: Keeps working and keeps her head down at Brannock. Asks the apprentice to show her any new tablet the firm brings in, and waits to see what the technology really does.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mainly for the young ones.
S1.quote: I teach him the stairs and he teaches me the screen.
S1.fieldNote: She blames tech companies, distant decision-makers, and any government that pays people to stay home rather than train. Her concern centres on apprenticeships, not her own job. She'd accept the role reversal with good humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing building work. Lord help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and somebody ought to slow it down. I'd say it after church, at the shop, to anyone. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty and I'd have no idea what to do. If robots can build an extension cheaper, people round here will use them, money's money. Three months of savings and no pension till sixty-six, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brannock as long as Rob would have me, and I think he'd try. We'd cut right back, no holiday, the car would have to last. And we'd lean on family, our son Mark has a decent job at the water company, and the church would help if it came to that, though I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be praying a lot more, I'll tell you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate asking for help. Would you take government support if it was there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather work. I've never taken a penny I didn't earn. But if the work's gone and the government's giving something to tide people over, I wouldn't let my pride starve us, I suppose. I'd feel ashamed, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much time. What would you do the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to Henrik and Rob. Rob would be honest with me, he always is. And I'd go to the vicar, not for money, just to talk, because I'd need someone to tell me it'll be all right even if they don't know.

S2.say: This is going too fast and somebody ought to slow it down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd say it to anyone and sign a letter.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with no idea what to do, and if robots build extensions cheaper, people round here will use them. Three months of savings and no pension till sixty-six is frightening.
S2.do: Keeps working at Brannock as long as she's wanted, cuts the holiday and keeps the old car. Leans on her son and, reluctantly, her church, and would take government support only if the work was truly gone.
S2.feel: Frightened, and praying a lot more.
S2.quote: I wouldn't let my pride starve us, I suppose. I'd feel ashamed, mind you.
S2.fieldNote: Her values clash with her situation: she dislikes handouts but admits she'd take support rather than go hungry, with shame. She'd turn to family, her employer and her vicar for reassurance. Her free-market view shows when she accepts that customers will choose the cheaper option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's use it to keep training young people in real trades. I'd say firms should take on more apprentices, not fewer. That's what I'd want people to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably get to sixty-three with Brannock, and then call it a day early on a smaller pension. It's not what I wanted, but we'd get by. Henrik's got his workshop and a bit of private pension, and we don't need much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, an extra sixty or seventy a month. I'd keep working and keep teaching Owen everything I know, faster. And I'd talk to Henrik about retiring together at sixty-three instead of me going on alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you teach Owen faster, if robots are coming anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a trade is never wasted. Even if robots build the houses, somebody needs to know when they've done it wrong. And Owen will have his whole life left, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get closer to the pension, and time to say goodbye to it properly. In two years it'd be snatched. In five, I could finish the stairs on my last job and walk away on my own two feet.

S3.say: There's time, so let's use it to keep training young people in real trades. Firms should be taking on more apprentices, not fewer.
S3.think: I'd probably get to sixty-three with Brannock and then retire early on a smaller pension. It's not what I wanted, but with Henrik's workshop and private pension we'd get by.
S3.do: Saves an extra sixty or seventy a month and keeps working at Brannock. Teaches the apprentice faster and plans with her husband to retire together at sixty-three.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with time to pray and plan.
S3.quote: In five, I could finish the stairs on my last job and walk away on my own two feet.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years matter to her mainly for dignity: leaving rather than being pushed. She believes a trade is never wasted, even with robots. Her retirement plan becomes a shared one with her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, with more grandchildren I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make sure young people still learn to work with their hands. I'd want apprenticeships protected, and families still able to stand on their own feet. I'd vote for whoever said that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's after my time, so I'd be all right. I'd retire at sixty-six like I planned. But I'd worry about my grandchildren, what they'll do with their days if machines do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different for me. Work at Brannock, retire at sixty-six, sing in the choir. I'd tell my grandson Toby to learn a proper trade anyway, something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, for the grandchildren. Not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about for the grandchildren, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they'd grow up with nothing to do and no reason to get up. Work isn't just money, it's how you know you're worth something. I don't know what a world without that looks like, and I don't think anyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it meant fewer men and women with ruined backs at sixty, I'd welcome that. Mr Brannock could barely walk at the end. But I'd want people still making things, somehow.

S4.say: We've got ten years to make sure young people still learn to work with their hands. I'd want apprenticeships protected and families able to stand on their own feet, and I'd vote for whoever said that.
S4.think: It's after my time, so I'd be all right, retiring at sixty-six as planned. But I'd worry about what my grandchildren will do with their days if machines do everything.
S4.do: Changes nothing for herself: works at Brannock, retires at sixty-six and keeps singing in the choir. Votes for candidates who protect apprenticeships and urges her grandson to learn a trade.
S4.feel: A little uneasy for the grandchildren, not for herself.
S4.quote: Work isn't just money, it's how you know you're worth something.
S4.fieldNote: Financially safe here, she worries about meaning rather than money for the next generation. She honestly admits she can't picture that world. She'd welcome fewer ruined backs, remembering her own mentor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be sixty with no pension, and no time to plan or even to say goodbye to the work properly. What would help is firms like Brannock being helped to keep people on, and apprenticeships kept going, rather than money handed out. And family, of course, family's what gets you through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Some people would laugh, but when I picture the worst of these, the first thing I'd do is go to church. Not because God fixes jobs, but because it reminds you that you're more than what you do for money.

headlineQuote: Not because God fixes jobs, but because it reminds you that you're more than what you do for money.
portrait: Elena Hansen is a 58-year-old carpenter who has spent twenty-two years with Brannock and Sons, a small family builder, and is teaching their apprentice the trade as she was taught. She never uses AI, sings in her church choir and minds her grandchildren on Saturdays. She is calm if AI fades and uneasy for apprentices under steady change. The two-year AGI picture alarms her, and she admits she'd swallow her pride and accept help rather than go hungry. With more time she plans to leave with dignity, and her worry turns to what work will mean for her grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be sixty with no pension and no time to plan or leave her work properly.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small firms like Brannock to keep people on, protected apprenticeships rather than handouts, and her family.
